d: Having or resembling repeated square indentations like those in a battlement
ety: From Medieval Latin castellātus (“fortified, castellate”) + -ed (forming past participles). Equivalent to the past participle of castellate but attested earlier than other uses of the verb.
s: Finally he walked slowly into a vast Italian space, with towers and castellated roofs, and a sky the colour of dark blue ink, smooth and consistent.

d: Marked by care and persistent effort
ety: A learned borrowing from Latin assiduus, from assidere (“to sit down to”), from ad- (“to”) + sedere (“to sit”). Compare sedulous. Cognate (via assidere) to assess.
s: A good deal of assiduous attention had enabled Henry to win this place in her affections.

d: A widow holding property received from her deceased husband
ety: From Middle French douagere, douagiere, from douage (“dower”), from the verb douer (“to endow”), from Latin dōtō (“to endow”), from dōs (“dowry”).
s: A reclusive dowager owned the pastures across the river, and her farmhands ran beef cattle on them.

d: Lacking cordiality; unfriendly
ety: From off + -ish.
s: Women on Reddit are sharing after how many dates/amount of time seeing each other they made it offish.

d: Roundabout and unnecessarily wordy; (‘ambagious’ is archaic)
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek περιφραστικός (periphrastikós), from περίφρασις (períphrasis, “periphrasis”).
s: He wrote a periphrastic love letter to his wife to patch up their relationship.

d: A kitchen servant employed to do menial tasks (especially washing)
ety: Either from Middle French escouillon (“a swab, cloth”), diminutive of escouve (“broom, twig”) from Latin scopa, or an alteration of Old French souillon (“scullion”) by influence of scullery.
s: "How now, you scullions and cullions: bring hither a pair of cow's hooves to out face this contumelious caitiff."

d: A quality that arouses emotions (especially pity or sorrow)
ety: From Ancient Greek πάθος (páthos, “suffering”).
s: His voice had a genuine pathos now, and his large brown hands perceptibly trembled.

d: Bend the knees and bow in church or before a religious superior or image
ety: From around 1620–1630 from Medieval Latin genūflectō (“to bend the knee”) equivalent to the Latin genū (“knee”) + flectō (“to bend”).
s: At high Mass the deacon and subdeacon stand on either side, genuflect too, and answer.

d: A statement that deviates from or perverts the truth
ety: Borrowed from Latin praevāricātiō (“collusion with an opponent; duplicity, deceit; violation of duty, transgression”, literally “stepping out of line”), from praevāricor (“to walk crookedly; go astray; transgress”) + -tās. The virtually obsolete sense of deviation or transgression may have been influenced by an earlier stage of borrowing via Middle English prevaricacioun, prevaricacion (“deviation
s: Prevarication became the order of the day in his government while truth was a stranger in those halls.

d: Having a pleasant sound
ety: From euphonical + -ous (suffix forming adjectives denoting possession or presence of a quality, commonly in abundance). Euphonical is derived from euphonic + -al (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’); with euphonic from euphony + -ic (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’), and euphony borrowed from French euphonie, from Ancient Greek εὐφωνία (eu
s: After casting about for some time for a name which should be worthy of her, he decided in favour of Sophronia Sphynx, as being euphonious and genteel, and furthermore indicative of mystery.

d: A tall upright megalith; found primarily in England and northern France
s: On the coast tree ferns and pandanus palms. Inland termite menhirs seventeen feet high.

d: Someone who is unimportant but cheeky and presumptuous
ety: From Middle English iack napys, iac nape, iac napes (“derogatory nickname of the English military commander and statesman William de la Pole, 1st Duke of Suffolk (1396–1450)”), probably from Jacun or Jakin (“pet forms of the male name Jack”) + ape (“ape, monkey”) + -s (possibly modelled after surnames such as Hobbes and Jakkes), referring to Suffolk’s heraldic badge which was an ape’s chain and cl
s: Who were the aristocracy, to give themselves airs? Jackanapes!

d: A pot that holds 2 quarts
ety: From Middle English potell, potel, from Old French potel, diminutive of pot; see more at pot.
s: Outside, I ripped open the bag to reveal the chips were sitting inside a paper pottle. A pottle!

d: Corrupt morally or by intemperance or sensuality
ety: From Latin vitiātus, the perfect passive participle of vitiō (“damage, spoil”), from vitium (“vice”).
s: There was excellent blood in his veins—royal stuff; though sadly vitiated, I fear, by the cannibal propensity he nourished in his untutored youth.

d: A style of popular music in the 1950s; based on American folk music and played on guitars and improvised percussion instruments
ety: From or related to Scots skiffle, from skiff (whence English skiff (“light rain, snow, etc”), which see for more). Related to skift (“light dusting of snow”).
s: They've been skiffling as we talked about in last chapter, and can now play a bit so their interests are broadening.

d: Surrender under agreed conditions
ety: The adjective is first attested in 1528, the verb in 1537; borrowed from Medieval Latin capitulātus perfect passive participle of Medieval Latin capitulō (“(originally; of a book, text) to draw up under distinct headings; (from the 15ᵗʰ c.) to bargain, parley, convene”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from capitulum (“heading, chapter, title”) + -ō (verb-formi
s: He argued and hollered for so long that I finally capitulated just to make him stop.

d: The language or speech of one individual at a particular period in life
ety: From idio- + -lect.
s: She perfected the fictional idiolect, fashioning habits of speaking for even minor characters that rendered them utterly singular.

d: A persistently annoying person
ety: From blight (something that impedes development or growth, or spoils any other aspect of life) + -er.
s: I tackled the blighter squarely.

d: Varying in color when seen in different lights or from different angles
ety: From French chatoyant, present participle of chatoyer (“to iridesce, like a cat's eye”), from chat (“cat”, because of the reflective qualities of a cat's eye).
s: Cover a tin using two or more colors of chatoyant clay separated by black strips.

d: Sorrow for sin arising from fear of damnation
ety: From Old French contriciun (French contrition), from Latin contrītiō.
s: Kremlin officials have shown no signs of contrition.

d: A soft tufted cord used in embroidery
ety: Borrowed from French chenille. Doublet of canicule.
s: The house seemed unfamiliar in the dark stormy light; the red and purple glass of the front door made livid bruises on the linoleum; the green chenille curtain was like a veil of seaweed.

d: Highly decorated earthenware with a glaze of tin oxide
ety: From Italian maiolica, named after the Island of Mallorca (formerly known as Maiòlica), which was once a commerce center for work produced in Valencia, Spain. Doublet of Mallorca and Majorca.
s: I propose that we should spend our honeymoon at Baiae. I have a villa at Baiae. It is there that I keep my grandfather’s collection of majolica. The sun shines there always.

d: A cudgel made of hardwood (usually oak or blackthorn)
ety: From Irish sail éille (“shillelagh”, literally “cudgel of a thong”), altered to match the name of the village of Shillelagh (from Irish Síol Éalaigh (literally “descendants of Éalach”), because the forest near it provided wood from which such clubs could be made.
s: It beats all your guns and your rifles, / For it goes off whene'er you desire, / And it's sure to hit just what it aims at, / For shillelaghs they never miss fire.

d: A piece of body armor for the trunk; usually consists of a breastplate and back piece
ety: From French corselet, from cors, an archaic spelling of corps (“body”).
s: Strictly speaking, the word corcelet meant only that part which covered the body, but was generally used to express the whole suit, under the terms of a corselet furnished, or complete.

d: (of a horse) having horseshoes with projecting nails to prevent slipping
ety: From rough + shod.
s: The horses fell down three times, the roads being slippery, and we walked three miles to Linlithgow. There we waited two hours, to have the fresh horses roughshod.

d: Armor plate that protects the arm
ety: Borrowed from French brassard, from bras (“arm”). The form brasset is attested since at least 1676 (Scots brassat is attested since 1590); brassart since at least 1736, brassard since at least 1788.
s: Muslims found not wearing the white brassards as prescribed by the army were simply despatched on the spot.

d: Absence of moral or spiritual values
ety: From Middle English iniquite, jniquite (“evil, wickedness, iniquity; evil act; hostility, malevolence; hostile act; a calamity, misfortune”), from Old French iniquité (modern French iniquité (“iniquity”)), from Latin inīquitās (“iniquity; inequality, unfairness; inequity, injustice”), from inīquus (“unequal, uneven, unfair; disadvantageous, unfavourable; hostile, unkind; unsuitable; wicked, wrong”
s: The path of the righteous man is beset on all sides by the iniquities of the selfish and the tyranny of evil men.

d: Act of writing in code or cipher
ety: From Ancient Greek στεγανός (steganós, “cover, roof”) + -graphy.
s: Using the steganography tools available today, suspects can even hide data inside JPEGs and audio files.

d: A simple form inferred as the common basis from which related words in several languages can be derived by linguistic processes
ety: From Ancient Greek ἔτυμον (étumon, “the true sense of a word according to its origin”), from ἔτυμος (étumos, “true, real, actual”).
s: The resulting citation collection was databased and coded for meaning, etymon, and date range (earliest and latest occurrence found).

d: Large watertight chamber used for construction under water
ety: From coffer + dam. The dental dam sense was introduced in English by dentist Sanford Christie Barnum at New York City in 1864 (by metaphor), but after his century it was maintained only in languages other than English (for example, German Kofferdam as a loanword from 19th-century English).
s: The contractor for the cofferdams, &c., was an Englishman, as were the principle workmen, and all the machinery has been supplied from England.

d: Without qualification; used informally as (often pejorative) intensifiers
ety: A variant of errant, from Middle English erraunt [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman erraunt, from Old French errant, the present participle of errer (“to walk (to); to wander (to); (figuratively) to travel, voyage”), and then: * from Vulgar Latin iterō (compare Late Latin itinerō, itineror (“to travel, voyage”)), from Latin iter (“a route (including a journey, trip; a course; a path; a road)”),
s: He was a tight brisk little man, with the air of an arrant old Bachelor.

d: Wander aimlessly in search of pleasure
ety: 1809, from gallant (“wooing women”), originally in sense “to flirt”, broadened to mean “roaming without plan”.
s: Rather than sit and gawk at my nonadoring mother and sister, I gallivanted outdoors until it was time to hit the sack.

d: Inform (somebody) of something
ety: Borrowed from French appris, apprise, the past participle form of apprendre (“to learn; to teach”), from Middle French apprendre, aprendre (“to learn”), from Old French aprendre, aprandre (“to learn; to educate, teach”), from Latin apprēndere, a variant of apprehendere, adprehendere, the present active infinitives of apprehendō, adprehendō (“to lay hold upon, grab, grasp, seize, take; to apprehend
s: The ears apprise the brain of sound.

d: Attack as false or wrong
ety: Borrowed from Middle French impugner, from Latin impugnō, from im- + pugnō (“fight”), from pugnus (“fist”), as in English pugilism (“fighting with fists, boxing”).
s: For quotations using this term, see Citations:impugn.

d: A public register showing the details of ownership and value of land; made for the purpose of taxation
ety: Borrowed from French cadastre.
s: As page 1 of the accompanying text helpfully explains, "ichnographic plans are particularly well suited for cadastres" but reveal nothing of the ups and downs and tops of things.

d: An instance of boastful talk
ety: From French gasconnade, from Gascon (“native of Gascony”) + -ade, equivalent to Gascon (“native of Gascony”) + -ade, literally "to talk like a Gascon". See French gasconnade.
s: The message is a gamer's gasconade: We cheat, we steal, we eat your lunch.

d: Packed full to capacity
ety: From chock + -a- + block.
s: Fish is chockablock full of protein.

d: A variable color averaging a vivid red
ety: From French carmin, from irregular Medieval Latin carminium, itself from Arabic قِرْمِز (qirmiz, “crimson, kermes”) from Persian *کرمست (*kermest), ultimately from Proto-Indo-Iranian *kŕ̥miš (“worm”), plus or with influence from Latin minium. Compare crimson and kermes.
s: He wore a great coat in midsummer, being affected with the trembling delirium, and his face was the color of carmine.

d: A deliberate pretense or exaggerated display
ety: From Middle French affectation and its etymon Latin affectātiōnem, from affectō (“to feign”). By surface analysis, affect + -ation.
s: This poem is strongly tinctured with those pedantic affectations concerning the passion of love ...

d: Cross or intersect so as to form a cross
ety: The adjective is first attested in 1825, the verb in 1658. Borrowed from Latin decussātus, perfect passive participle of decussō (“to divide crosswise, arrange crosswise or mark with a cross”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from decussis (“a coin worth ten asses; a cross sign (from the cross shape of the Roman numeral for ten carved on the coins)”), from dece
s: The two trochlears decussate in the anterior medullary velum.
